did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah warns Israel not to follow the ways of the nations and not to fear the signs in the sky, because fearing them is characteristic of the nations, not of those who worship the Lord.
Did you know? The chapter describes idols as a tree cut down in the forest and shaped by a craftsman, emphasizing that they are human creations rather than divine powers.
Did you know? Idols are portrayed as lifeless figures that cannot speak or walk and can do neither harm nor good; therefore, there is no reason to fear them.
Did you know? Jeremiah draws a sharp contrast between idols and the Lord: the Lord is the true God, the living God, and the everlasting King, while the nations’ statues are lifeless.
Did you know? Verse 11 appears in Aramaic and declares that the gods who did not make the heavens and the earth will perish from the earth and from under the heavens.
Did you know? The chapter attributes control over natural phenomena to the Lord: he makes the clouds rise, produces lightning with the rain, and brings out the wind from his storehouses.
Did you know? Unlike the idols, Jacob’s portion is the Lord, because he is the one who formed everything; Israel is also described as the tribe of his inheritance.

Did you know? The scattering of the flock and the destruction described in the chapter are linked to the shepherds—that is, the leaders—who did not seek the Lord and therefore failed to lead the flock wisely.
Did you know? Jeremiah acknowledges that people do not determine their own path entirely and cannot direct their own steps by themselves; this expresses humanity’s dependence on the Lord.
Did you know? The prophet prays that the Lord will discipline his people with measure and justice, not in anger, which could diminish and destroy them.
